blocks.text: Anthropic 想两头兼顾。随着即将到来的 IPO，它既想利用公开市场的巨额财富，又坚称不愿牺牲其核心使命——安全地开发 AI 并造福人类。但更强的模型能力会带来更大的风险，而渴望回报的股东可能对拖慢产品上市进程、成本高昂的安全措施缺乏耐心。

blocks.text: 宾夕法尼亚大学法学教授 Elizabeth Pollman 对The Verge表示，Anthropic 提议以“一种前所未有的、独特而复杂的治理结构”上市，该结构是“为这家创始人主导、使命驱动的公司精心设计的”。专家表示，这应能让 Anthropic 自由追求利润，同时不让股东迫使它在安全上偷工减料，或在系统得到充分测试之前就仓促推出。但再强的法律保护也有其限度，无论设计得多么完善，没有任何公司结构能让一家上市公司完全免受市场需求的左右。

blocks.text: 首先，Anthropic 是一家公益公司（public benefit corporation）。简而言之，法律要求它不能只专注于股东回报最大化，而要在其宣称的社会使命与员工、特定社区等利益相关方的利益之间取得平衡。Patagonia 和 Kickstarter 是较为知名的例子，其使命分别聚焦于环境保护和支持创意社区。

blocks.text: 另一项关键保障旨在通过限制股东对公司最大权力杠杆之一——董事会——的影响力来保护 Anthropic 的使命。董事负责监督公司并任命其领导层，包括 CEO。董事也可以兼任高管，Anthropic 就是如此，CEO Dario Amodei 和总裁 Daniela Amodei 均在董事会任职。

blocks.text: 股东通常对董事会人选拥有相当大的影响力，这使他们能够在不满公司运营方式时更换董事或推动变革。例如，如果股东认为可选的安全测试不必要地拖延了产品上市而感到不满，他们可能会罢免董事，换上更符合自身利益（比如赚钱、少些谨慎）的人。

blocks.text: 该信托由“五位与财务无利害关系的投票受托人”组成，他们在“AI安全、国家安全、公共政策和社会企业”方面拥有专业知识。通过一种名为T类股的特殊股份类别，受托人可以任命或罢免董事，以实现其既定目标：确保“Anthropic负责任地平衡股东的财务利益与受Anthropic行为及我们公共利益目标影响者的利益”。该信托旨在独立于公司的商业压力运作，理论上使其能够将Anthropic的使命放在首位。

blocks.text: 法律保护与免受市场压力之间存在很大区别。Lipton说，Anthropic像所有AI公司一样，“迫切需要资本”。“我不清楚任何治理结构能否抵御这一市场现实：除非Anthropic以比竞争对手更快的速度利用盈利机会，否则它将无法为其运营提供资金。”Lund表达了类似的担忧。她说，Anthropic仍将“需要保持在投资者的青睐之中”，并补充说“竞争压力和资本需求可能会随着时间的推移侵蚀安全承诺。”Anthropic未回应The Verge关于其是否认为公司能够真正抵御股东以牺牲安全为代价大幅加速AI的压力的问题。

blocks.text: Anthropic wants to have it both ways. With its impending IPO, it wants to tap the vast riches of the public markets and insists it doesn’t want to compromise its core mission of developing AI safely and for the benefit of humanity. But greater model capabilities bring greater risks, and shareholders eager for returns may have little patience for costly safety measures that slow products on their way to market.

blocks.text: University of Pennsylvania law professor Elizabeth Pollman told The Verge that Anthropic has proposed going public with a “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before” and that has been “creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” Experts say it should give Anthropic freedom to pursue profits without letting shareholders force it to cut corners on safety or rush systems out before they’re adequately tested. But even the strongest legal protections can only go so far, and no corporate structure, no matter how well designed, can completely insulate a public company from the demands of the market.

blocks.text: Foremost, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation. Simply put, it is legally required to focus on more than just maximizing shareholder returns, balancing these with its stated social mission and the interests of stakeholders, such as employees and specific communities. Patagonia and Kickstarter are among the better-known examples, with missions centered on environmental conservation and supporting creative communities, respectively.

blocks.text: Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, ordinary shareholders won’t have much of a say over who is on the board at all. Instead, four of the board’s seven directors will be chosen by a special body called the long-term benefit trust, explains Jens Dammann, a professor in business and commercial law at the University of Texas School of Law. It is a highly unusual setup for a major technology company.

Instead, four of the board’s seven directors will be chosen by a special body called the long-term benefit trust, explains Jens Dammann, a professor in business and commercial law at the University of Texas School of Law. It is a highly unusual setup for a major technology company.

blocks.text: The trust is made up of “five financially disinterested voting trustees” with expertise in “AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” Through a special class of share called Class T stock, the trustees can appoint or remove directors in pursuit of their stated purpose: ensuring “that Anthropic responsibly balances the financial interests of stockholders with the interests of those affected by Anthropic’s conduct and our public benefit purpose.” The trust is designed to operate independently of the company’s commercial pressures, allowing it, in theory, to put Anthropic’s mission first.

blocks.text: Ordinary shareholders technically have a say in the board’s three remaining seats. However, Anthropic has created another safeguard that keeps power firmly in the hands of its founders, called “Founder LLC,” which will control 50.1 percent of the voting power on shareholder matters. Given that many shareholder votes are decided by a simple majority, Founder LLC basically gives Anthropic’s founders the ability to block or force through decisions, regardless of how other shareholders vote. This means that they will effectively choose the remaining three directors, Columbia Law School professor Dorothy Lund told The Verge.

blocks.text: All in all, the arrangements would give Anthropic’s founders and the trust “tremendous power” over the company’s direction, shielding it from many of “the pressures associated with being a public company,” Dammann told The Verge. “Given the unusual governance structure Anthropic has chosen, I don’t see how going public, by itself, would undermine its ability to prioritize safety over commercial interests.”

blocks.text: Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School, agreed, telling The Verge that, legally speaking, “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” But Lipton cautioned that the founders themselves have financial stakes in the company, which could influence their decisions.

blocks.text: And there’s a big difference between legal protections and immunity from market pressures. Anthropic, like all AI companies, “desperately needs capital,” Lipton said. “It’s not clear to me that any governance structure will protect against the market reality that unless Anthropic takes advantage of profit making opportunities at a faster pace than its competitors, it will not be able to fund its operations.” Lund expressed similar concerns. Anthropic will still “need to stay in the good graces of their investors,” she said, adding that “competitive pressure and capital needs can erode safety commitments over time.” Anthropic did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment on whether it felt the company could actually resist shareholder pressure to massively accelerate AI at the cost of safety.

blocks.text: Another potential vulnerability emerges if Anthropic’s founders start leaving. In its prospectus, the company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly its founders. Dario and Daniela are singled out as being especially “critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. But beyond the loss of leadership, their departure could trigger significant changes in how the company is structured, potentially stripping away some of the safeguards preventing Anthropic from pursuing profit over safety.

blocks.text: Under the proposed structure, Founder LLC would “sunset” if a majority of its members leave or the group chooses to dissolve it. Once that happens, ordinary shareholders could gain the power to weaken the trust’s protections, even against the wishes of the trustees, and without the support of the founders or employees, who hold different classes of stock, Dammann told The Verge. Other means of subverting the trust also exist, he explained, including coordinated action by the public shareholders, employee stockholders, and founders.

blocks.text: For now, it seems, Anthropic can probably have it both ways. But the protections designed to preserve its commitment to AI safety are far from ironclad, and much depends on market pressures, whether its founders stick around, and directions of the trust. Dammann said he sees a “fundamental dilemma that cannot be resolved in a fully satisfactory way” between Anthropic’s mission and investor demands. As long as things are going well, this tension may be manageable. “Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well,” Dammann said. “But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.”
